lines.note: Completes xicai-uo from the preceding page: the example concerns governing the world after receiving the general's command. Qir. is an upright citation label; the italic translation starts with Ouindo, not inside that label.

runs.text: Capitão general, pos, ou gouernou em paz o mũ

lines.note: The general's command is followed by establishing or governing the world in peace. The printed mũ is an abbreviated first part of mundo, continued by do on the next row; no unprinted terminal hyphen has been supplied.

The opening do completes mundo. The paragraph then gives receiving God's punishment, with the humble compound macari cǒmuru divided at cǒmu-; Deus is part of the Japanese example, not the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: Receber o pago, ou castigo de Deos por

lines.note: The final ru completes cǒmuru. The Portuguese explicitly allows either recompense or punishment from God, specifying an offence on the following row; retain the printed castigo rather than normalizing its s-allograph.
Completes the preceding definition with 'for some crime.' This short continuation belongs to Macaricǒmuri across the page boundary, not to the new Macaricoxi entry below.

Macaricoxi is the humble verb for going or coming to a place, here glossed as passing or going somewhere. The inflectional series ſu, oita is clearly printed and is not regularized to a different romanization.
Introduces a deliberate visit to pay respects: Vazato vonreini macaricoite. The full initial V belongs to the upright Japanese example; the italic introductory Vt ends before that word.

The example promises to speak or offer thanks, followed by the Mon. citation. The damaged OCR irebzu is read ireôzu from the long-vowel mark and letter shapes; the Portuguese propoſi- continues as to on the next row.

runs.text: to a vos ver falarei, ou darei as graças.

lines.note: Completes 'coming expressly to see you, I shall speak or give thanks.' The Portuguese alternatives clarify the preceding Japanese phrase without changing its historical spelling.
Macaricudari means to descend or come down, exemplified by leaving Miyaco. Miyaco occurs within the italic Portuguese explanation here and is a whole-word typeface-review candidate.
The Japanese example begins 'when I came down from Miyaco.' Its to- continues as qi on the next row, and Miyacoyori remains a single printed unit rather than being respaced from modern Japanese.

runs.text: qi, roxide cotono foca xinrǒ ximaraxita.

lines.note: Completes toqi and describes exceptional difficulty on the journey. The scan supports roxide, xinrǒ and ximaraxita; these historical forms are retained rather than recast as modern Japanese conjugations.

runs.text: Quando deci do Miyaco leuei muito

lines.note: The Mon. citation precedes the translation 'when I came down from Miyaco, I underwent much ...'. Miyaco is embedded in the Portuguese explanation and remains in its printed italic setting.
Completes the preceding translation with 'trouble.' The one-word row is genuine continuation text, not a separate entry or a displaced catchword.
Macari ide is glossed as going outside. The space between Macari and ide is visible; retain this separately printed form rather than merging it to match the following variant.
Macarijde is an immediately following joined variant with the same meaning. The j-form and absence of a space are printed distinctions, not reasons to duplicate the preceding spelling mechanically.
Macarimodori means to return. The compact Portuguese Tornarſe supplies the reflexive sense, and the inflectional ending otta is preserved.
Macarimucai means to go to meet someone. Both long-vowel signs in ǒ, ǒta are retained as printed; the headword and conjugational forms remain upright.
Macarinari is 'to become,' and the example begins with Con-nen, 'this year.' Preserve the physical hyphen rather than combining the example across the two printed rows.
The example says that the speaker becomes fifty years old this year. The visible gojǔni replaces malformed OCR gojfini; the Mon. citation is followed by the beginning of the Portuguese translation.

runs.text: anno faço cincoenta annos de idade. ¶

lines.note: Completes the age statement as fifty years, then begins a separate example Faca-nǒ. This is the start of the euphemistic expression explained as dying on the next row, not a Portuguese word.
Completes Facanǒ macari natta, glossed simply as 'died.' The past form natta is supported by the paired t shapes and the expression's grammar; the OCR nauta is not retained.
Macarinobori is the humble verb for going up. The example starts Coco-motoye, 'to here,' and the first part stays at the right edge of this physical row.
The example describes coming up here suddenly, followed by the Mon. label. The Portuguese De- continues as repente; the historical futto is retained as printed.
Completes the explanation 'suddenly I came, or came up, here.' The row starts with the continuation of De-repente and does not introduce an independent headword.
Macarinoqi means to withdraw or move away. The Portuguese alternative afas-tarſe is physically divided; the inflection oita is not altered on the basis of a modern spelling.
Completes afastarſe, the second Portuguese equivalent of Macarinoqi. This small row is body text and keeps its indentation and final period.

Macariſugui means to pass or go by. The example starts Co-coro narazu, introducing something that passed contrary to one's wishes; the long s in the headword remains distinct from the Portuguese double-s ligature.

runs.text: coro narazu macari ſuguite gozaru, atono

lines.note: The example says the event has passed unwillingly or beyond the speaker's control and then turns to earlier discourtesy. Its printed spaces and comma after gozaru are preserved rather than reorganized as a modern sentence.
The speaker humbly requests pardon for earlier discourtesy. The nasal mark over gomẽ is visible and restored; arǒzu retains its caron, and Mon. is an upright citation label.

runs.text: Paſſou ſem ſer mais em minha mão, os a-

lines.note: The translation says it happened beyond the speaker's power and begins a-grauos, 'offences.' Retain the physical break and the source's formulation rather than smoothing its Portuguese syntax.
Completes a plea to forgive former offences. The closely set meperdoeis and absence of a clear closing full stop are retained as printed; no punctuation is added merely to finish the sentence.
Macaritachi means to rise or depart. The Portuguese par-tirſe is divided at the row end, and the following example distinguishes a reason for getting up.
The example begins a statement about not offering more wine. Goxuuo is part of the upright Japanese sentence; the italic Vt belongs to the introduction, not to that example.
Completes the negative past macaritatananda and gives the Mon. citation. The entire label, including its period, is upright; the Portuguese explanation then begins 'I did not get up ...'.

runs.text: uantei pera que vos não conuidaſſe mais cõ vi-

lines.note: The explanation continues with not inviting the addressee to more wine. The nasal abbreviation cõ is printed, and vi- continues as nho on the next physical row.
Completes vinho and adds 'but for another reason.' This clause belongs to the Macaritachi example and retains the old spelling reſpeito.
Macaritçuqi means to arrive. The Portuguese initial is C in Chegar, not the OCR G; the cedilla in the Japanese romanization and the past form uita are retained.
Macaritodomari means to remain or be detained. The short definition Deterſe and the inflectional series u, atta are read together rather than expanding the entry with an inferred example.
Macaritouori means to pass by. The example begins Maca-ritouoru on this row; the physical division belongs to the headword's use in the example, not to a new lexical item.

runs.text: ritouoru ſô cono vonfudauo fijte maitta.

lines.note: The example describes a passing monk coming after taking the written notice. The scan supports ſô and fijte; retain the printed j-form and the spelling vonfudauo rather than replacing them with a modern transcription.
After the Mon. citation the Portuguese identifies a travelling Buddhist monk who was passing. Bonzo is the source's Portuguese term; the label remains upright and the gloss italic.
Completes the account of taking the written board and coming. The historical forms taboa and veo are retained, with no inserted accents or modernization.
Macariyori means to approach. The example begins Toxi, 'age/years,' preparing the idiomatic sense of advancing in age on the following row.
Completes Toxi macariyoru, glossed as becoming old. The printed compound's spacing is retained rather than forcing it to match the headword's capitalization.
Macaxe means to leave something to another's will. The nasal abbreviations algũa and võ- are printed; the latter continues as tade below.
Completes 'another's will' and introduces Cocoroni macaſuru. Its Portuguese Fa- continues as zer at the top of column 2; the column transition does not omit a line or require a new entry.

runs.text: zer a couſa conforme a ſua vontade.

lines.note: Completes Fa-zer from the bottom of column 1: doing something according to one's own will. The continuation belongs to Cocoroni macaſuru and is correctly placed before the next headword.

Maccaiſamani is an adverb meaning completely the other way round. The Portuguese aueſas has the printed single long s, and the historical Japanese form is not replaced with the more familiar modern sakasama.

The example concerns accusing someone contrary to what occurred. Both t letters are visible in vttayuru, correcting the OCR's single-t vtayuru; the paragraph sign is retained separately from the upright example.

runs.text: guem ao contrario do que paſſou.

lines.note: Completes the statement that the accusation reverses what actually happened. The row begins the continuation al-guem and retains the source's Portuguese orthography.
Maccha is identified with Fiqicha and glossed as ground tea. The synonym following i, remains ordinary Japanese text, not an embedded-Portuguese typeface term; no modern accent is added to Cha.

runs.text: Certa folha, ou caſca de aruore moida

lines.note: This Maccǒ denotes a particular leaf or bark ground up. The caron on the final vowel is printed; the description continues onto the next row and is distinct from the following homograph concerning a helmet.

runs.text: em poo que queimão diante do Pagode.

lines.note: Completes the definition as powder burned before the religious image. The printed poo and Pagode are preserved; the wording is the dictionary's historical description, not a botanical identification supplied by the reviewer.
A second Maccǒ is exemplified by Cabutono maccǒ, the front part of a helmet. The example remains upright, and the Portuguese di- continues as anteira below.
Completes dianteira do capacete, 'the front of the helmet.' This is the final row of the second Maccǒ entry, not part of the adverbial headword that follows.

runs.text: Adu. De fronte, ou diante do

lines.note: Maccǒni is the adverb 'directly in front,' specifically before the face. The printed Adu. is italic; the caron distinguishes the source's marked long vowel without modernizing its value.
Completes roſto and begins an example of drawing a sword and holding it directly in front. Catanauo and the remaining Japanese sentence are upright after the italic Vt.

The example continues by raising the sword and rushing forward with vigorous movement. Retain the printed momini môde and its circumflex rather than silently inserting a nasal consonant; Deſ- begins the Portuguese translation across the row break.

runs.text: embainhando a Catana, & aleuantandoa de frõ

lines.note: Completes Deſembainhando and says the sword was raised in front. Catana is embedded within the Portuguese explanation; frõ is a nasal abbreviation continued by te on the next row, with no invented terminal hyphen.

runs.text: te da testa, chegouſe muito de preßa meneando

lines.note: Completes fronte and describes approaching very quickly while moving the arms. The source's testa spelling and preßa ligature are retained, together with the unhyphenated chegouſe.
Completes the preceding description with 'the arms.' The short body continuation is not a headword or furniture item and keeps its final period.
Maccurona describes something thoroughly or truly black. The qualifier verdadei-ramente spans this row and the next, and the headword's double c is preserved.
Completes the definition of absolute blackness and begins an example about black clothing. Maccurona detachino remains the upright Japanese example after the paragraph sign.
The example says that there were also people dressed thus, followed by the Mon. citation. The caron in xǔmo and the Portuguese spacing tam bem are retained from the scan.
Completes al-gũs and the statement that some wore entirely black dress. The nasal abbreviation gũs belongs to the Portuguese continuation rather than a separate lexical item.

Maccuroni is the corresponding adverb, initially glossed as in black or truly black. The long Portuguese verdadeira- continues on the next row; do not confuse this entry with the adjectival form above.

runs.text: mente preto, l, rija, ou ſeueramente. Vt,

lines.note: Adds the figurative senses firmly or severely and introduces an accusation example. The right-edge Mac- is a hyphenated fragment of Mac-curoni, not the full stop produced by OCR.
Completes Maccuroni vttayuru, 'to accuse strongly and severely.' The double t agrees with the visible example earlier in this column, and ſeue- continues as ramente below.
Completes ſeueramente. This single-word continuation closes the figurative Maccuroni example before the first noun Machi.

runs.text: Ruas de caſas que vão continuadas,

lines.note: The first noun Machi is defined as continuous rows or streets of houses. The dictionary's explanation begins with the physical arrangement rather than directly equating the word with a modern municipality.

runs.text: & ainda que eſte he o proprio ſẽ

lines.note: Says the houses stand in line and calls this the word's proper sense. The abbreviated ſẽ continues as tido on the next row; retain the colon and ampersand as printed.

runs.text: tido desta palaura, tambem ſe toma no vulgo

lines.note: Completes ſẽtido and contrasts this primary sense with common usage. The historical palaura and the source's st-allograph in desta are not modernized.
Completes the broader popular meanings: settlement, town or city. The row closes the first Machi entry and must remain separate from the garment-related homograph below.

runs.text: Neſgas que ſe acrecentão nos calçoẽs

lines.note: The second noun Machi denotes gussets added to breeches. The printed calçoẽs and acrecentão are retained rather than changed to modern Portuguese spelling.

runs.text: pera os fazer por baixo mais largos, & foiga-

lines.note: Explains that the gussets make the lower portion wider and looser. Second-pass enlargement supports a dotted i-like type in foiga-, unlike the taller l in largos on the same row. The aligned reading foiga- is therefore retained with a nonblocking damaged-letter/printing-anomaly caveat, not silently emended to the expected folga-.
Completes the description and gives Facamano machiuo iruru, inserting gussets into hakama. The Japanese example is upright; the Portuguese Me- continues as ter below.

runs.text: ter estas neſgas antre as pernas dos calçoẽs.

lines.note: Completes the instruction to put these gussets between the legs of the breeches. The old forms estas, antre and calçoẽs are preserved rather than linguistically normalized.

runs.text: Abertura do ferro de duas pontas da

lines.note: The third noun Machi refers to the opening between the two points of an iron arrowhead. The definition continues with frecha on the next row; it is not the garment sense above.
Completes the arrow-related definition. The source uses frecha, which is retained rather than changed to modern flecha.
The verb Machi, with tçu and atta, means to wait. This is a separate verbal entry following three nouns of the same printed spelling.
Machiacaxi means to wait throughout the night. The tightly set anoite is retained, together with the printed inflection aita and the long s in ſu.
Machiauaxe means for people to wait for one another. The nasal abbreviation hũs is printed, and pel- continues as los on the next row rather than being modernized to pelos.
Completes pellos outros, 'for the others.' This continuation closes the reciprocal-waiting definition and preserves the historical doubled l across the row division.

Machibuxe means an ambush; the Portuguese notes a Ximo regional alternative, Fuxi-cuſa. Ximo is embedded in the explanation, whereas the upright regional synonym after the comma is not marked merely because it adjoins Portuguese.
Completes Fuxicuſa and gives Machibuxeuo ſuru, 'to make an ambush.' The Portuguese ci- continues as lada below; neither Japanese expression is resegmented from modern spelling.
Completes cilada, ending the ambush example. The one-word continuation retains its printed alignment and does not absorb the new Machicane entry beneath it.
Machicane means to have difficulty waiting. Two f letters are visible in difficul-, matching the spelling in the example's translation below; the OCR's single f is corrected.
The example concerns being unable to wait for the year to end. Sono toxino cururuuo and the physical machi- break are preserved; cururu is not replaced with a modern form.
Completes machicaneſaxerareta and gives the Yam. citation. The explanation again begins 'had difficulty'; the citation label is upright and the Portuguese difficul- continues below.

runs.text: dade de eſperar que ſe acabaße o anno.

lines.note: Completes the explanation as having difficulty waiting until the year ended. The printed acabaße ligature remains unchanged, and the row's final period closes the example.

Machicaqe means to wait alertly or in readiness. Enlargement supports the acute accent in á lerta. The source's final dotted i-like glyph is retained in eſperandoi from the aligned draft, despite the expected Portuguese eſperando; this is a nonblocking damaged/possibly erroneous glyph, not a silently corrected word.

runs.text: Monguchi made mina dete vare ſaqin

lines.note: The example describes everyone coming out as far as the entrance, each trying to be first. The printed vare ſaqin is retained without expanding or modernizing its final form.

Completes the example and gives Mon., then begins the Portuguese 'all coming out to the ...'. The isolated por- beneath the body is a catchword anticipating the next page, not part of this physical body row.
